title: Electric Circuits and Energy Transfer
summary: Components and circuit diagrams, conductors and insulators, energy transfer in circuits, and how series and parallel circuits behave.

notes.text: An **electric circuit** is a complete, unbroken path through which electric current can flow. Every circuit needs an **energy source** (a cell or battery), **conducting wires** and at least one **component** that uses the energy (a bulb, motor, buzzer). A **switch** opens and closes the circuit.
The flow of charge (electrons) through a conductor. It is measured in **amperes (A)** with an **ammeter**.

items: **Conductors** allow current to flow easily: metals such as copper, aluminium and iron, and graphite (pencil lead).
**Insulators** do not allow current to flow: plastic, rubber, glass, wood and dry air. Wires are coated in plastic for safety.

notes.title: Testing materials
notes.problem: A learner places a steel nail, a plastic ruler, a copper coin and a rubber band in the gap of a circuit with a bulb. Predict which light the bulb.
steps: A material must let charges flow to complete the circuit.
Metals are conductors: steel and copper.
Plastic and rubber are insulators, so no current flows.
notes.answer: The bulb lights for the nail and the coin only.

notes.text: The cell stores **chemical potential energy**. When the circuit is closed, this is transferred as electrical energy to the components, which convert it into useful forms. Some energy is always wasted, usually as heat.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Adding more **cells in series** makes bulbs brighter (more energy pushes the current). Adding more **bulbs in series** makes them dimmer, because the total resistance increases and less current flows.
How much a component opposes the flow of current. Thin, long wires and materials like nichrome have high resistance; resistance causes energy to be converted to heat.

notes.label: Safety
notes.text: A **short circuit** happens when current flows through a path with almost no resistance, for example when the two terminals of a cell are joined directly by a wire. A very large current flows, the wire becomes hot and the cell runs flat quickly. In a house this can cause fires; fuses and circuit breakers cut the current.

notes.title: When one bulb blows
notes.problem: Two bulbs are connected to a battery, first in series and then in parallel. One bulb blows in each circuit. What happens to the other?
steps: In series there is only one path, so a break stops the current everywhere.
In parallel each bulb has its own path to the battery, so the other path stays complete.
notes.answer: In series the other bulb goes out. In parallel it stays lit.

questions.explanation: A series circuit has only one path, so a break stops all current.

questions.prompt: Explain why two bulbs connected in series with one cell glow less brightly than one bulb on its own.
questions.memo:
✓ The total resistance of the circuit increases (1)
✓ so less current flows / the energy from the cell is shared between two bulbs (1)

questions.prompt: What is a short circuit and why is it dangerous?
questions.memo:
✓ Current flows through a path with very low resistance, bypassing the components (1)
✓ A very large current flows, which makes wires hot and can cause fires / flattens the battery (1)

questions.prompt: Give TWO reasons why houses are wired in parallel.
questions.memo:
✓ If one appliance is switched off or breaks, the others still work (1)
✓ Each appliance gets the full voltage / works at full power (1)
